title-group.article-title: A support vector machine approach for identification of pleural effusion

contrib-group.aff: Department of Physics, Faculty of Science and Mathematics, Diponegoro University, Semarang, Indonesia

abstract.p: In this research, we investigated the method which was based on a support vector machine (SVM) to identify pleural effusion on the thoracic image. SVM is a method of machine learning that works well when applied to data outside the training set. We formulated the detection of pleural effusion and applied SVM to develop the identification algorithm. We applied SVM to detect thoracic images whether they identified as pleural effusion or normal. The identification of pleural effusion on the thoracic image was conducted through some processes such as the determination of the region of interest (ROI), segmentation, morphology operation, measurement of the sharpness value and slope value, training as well as testing. Determining ROI was intended to focus the measurement on the left side of the chest. Segmentation was carried out to separate lungs object from the background. Morphology operation was carried out for cavities on the object as the segmentation result to obtain the entire object so that the measurement of the slope's lower part image could be done perfectly. The training was carried out on 100 thoracic images, 50 of them were identified with pleural effusion and the other 50 were normal. The objective was to find the hyperplane with the parameter input such as the sharpness value and slope value of the lungs on the thoracic image. We tested the method proposed based on doctors' diagnosis using 50 thoracic images, 25 of which were identified with pleural effusion and the other 25 were normal. From the result of the test, the accuracy of the method we proposed was 96%.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Support vector machine (SVM) is a learning machine for two groups of classification problems [1,2]. SVM learning has been used in many applications, some of them are the detection of object and classification in medical imagery [[3], [4], [5], [6], [7]], detection of object and classification in transportation system [[8], [9], [10]], gender classification [11], signature recognition [12] and detection of termites [13]. The formulation of SVM learning was based on the principles of structural risk minimization. SVM could be used to minimize the limitations of the generalization error so that it tended to work well when applied to the data outside the training set. In this research, we investigated the use of an SVM-based approach to classifying objects from a medical image. Specifically, we clarified the pleural effusion on the thoracic image.

The following was the reason for the use of the SVM-based approach to be classified as pleural effusion. Besides lungs cancer, brain tumor, and eye glaucoma, pleural effusion is also a serious disorder which has been a problem in the health sector. Pleura is a double layer from a thin tissue consisting of a mesothelial cell, connective tissue, capillary blood vessels, and lymph vessels. All tissues separate lungs from the chest wall and mediastinum. Pleural effusion could be caused by defects in lungs such as bacterial and virus infections [[14], [15], [16], [17]], cancer [[18], [19], [20]], transfer of fluid from intravascular into interstitial cavities such as kidney and liver, heart failure [[21], [22], [23], [24]], AIDS [25], and lupus [26]. Pleural effusion is also frequently caused by trauma and surgery. Pleural effusion restricts the ability of lungs to inflate and deflate as well as makes breathing harder.

Every year, the incidence of pleural effusion was estimated 1–1.5 million new cases in the US and 200–250,000 in England [27]. Pleural effusion could be detected through the conventional thoracic image [28]. X-ray images from thoracic were then analyzed and diagnosed by a radiology expert. The process of analyzing and diagnosing took a quite long time and the doctor also had some issues in the diagnosis process since the characteristic of pleural effusion was sometimes unclear, so that the determination was still subjective. For this reason, it took a method development to classify whether such a pleura was identified as effusion or not, automatically and it took a relatively shorter time.

In this paper, SVM was trained through learning to classify thoracic images based on two parameters, they were the sharpness value and slope value. This parameter is a novelty in this study and we hope to produce better accuracy than using other parameters, for example those resulting from feature extraction using GLCM [[29], [30], [31]]. These parameters are real and can be seen visually, but it is difficult to ask using a computer if it is only guided by feature extraction in the GLCM method, for example texture, contrast, homogeneity, entropy and so on. In terms of texture, contrast and homogeneity, the characteristics of the lungs suffering from pleural effusion and normal lungs are almost the same, it's just that in the lungs suffering from pleural effusion there is an accumulation of fluid which in the chest image produces a white area which causes the lower part of the lung to become flat. Both parameters were obtained based on the visual observation that the lower part of the normal lungs (not identified by the pleural effusion) would be sharp and tilted. If the lungs had pleural effusion, the lower part of the lungs would be blunt and flat since they were filled with fluid.

To make it easier for readers to follow this paper, we show the organization of this paper as follows. The introductory section provides a thorough overview of pleural effusion and the need for automated detection methods. The introduction also provides reasons why we use this SVM method. We have explained this in part I of this paper. The theory section explains theoretical matters related to SVM, pleural effusion, and image segmentation. We will explain this in part II of this paper. The methodology section describes the research material and the specific steps involved in the classification, namely: data collection for training and testing, segmentation, measurement of sharpness values, measurement of slope values, SVM implementation in the form of plotting sharpness versus slope values to obtain a hyperplane. How to verify the method is also explained in this section. We will explain this in part III of this paper. The results and discussion sections provide a description of the evaluation metrics used to assess the performance of the proposed method. This section will measure the accuracy, precision and recall of the test results for the proposed method. In addition, the limitations and challenges encountered during the testing phase will be discussed. We will explain this in part IV of this paper. Finally, the conclusion would be withdrawn in Part V.

sec.title: Support vector machine (SVM)
sec.p: SVM was known as the ultimate learning machine that has successfully been used in the recognition of image patterns [32]. The learning was carried out by using input and output data pairs in the form of the target intended. Such kind of learning is called supervised learning. With such directed learning, the function that describes the dependency of input and output. Further, the function obtained was expected to have a good generalization ability, which means that such a function could be used as input data outside the learning data [33].

SVM is a nonlinear classification that can classify the feature into two classes. The basic principles of SVM are linear classification, and further is developed so that it could work in nonlinear issue. The objective of SVM is to find the hyperplane between two classes in vector space [1]. SVM has two important processes, namely the pattern recognition process or training process and the verification process or testing process. The pattern recognition process would produce line that has become the separator between two classes which are right in the middle called a hyperplane. This particular line becomes a reference in the verification process. In the recognition of the SVM pattern, it takes an input parameter that has become the special characteristics between the two classes that would be separated. Such a parameter would later be categorized in class +1 or class −1 and becomes the pattern separating the two classes, SVM classification could be seen in Fig. 1.Fig. 1
SVM classification.Fig. 1

Fig. 1 displays some of the patterns which have become a member of the two classes i.e. +1 and −1. The pattern which was classified into class −1 was symbolized by a circle, while the pattern in class +1 is symbolized by a cross. The best separator between both classes could be found by measuring the margin of the separator and find its maximum point. Margin is the distance between such separators with the closest pattern from each class. The closest pattern is called a support vector. The full line in Fig. 1 shows the best separator, i.e the located exactly in the middle of both classes is the one called a hyperplane. The effort to find the location of this separator is the core of the learning process in SVM. The data available is denoted as x ∈Rd for i = 1,2,3, …, n, where n is the amount of data. Positive class is denoted as +1, and negative class as −1, then the data and label of the class are denoted as yi∋{−1,+1}. Further, it is assumed that both classes could be separated perfectly by a separator in the form of a straight line defined under the equations below [1]:(1)w→.x→+b=0

Pattern xi→ which is included in class −1 (negative class) could be formulated as the pattern that meets the inequality of:(2)w→.x→+b≤−1while pattern xi→ which is included in class +1 (positive class):(3)w→.x→+b≥+1

The margin between the line of the class separator is 2||w||. The biggest margin could be found by maximizing the margin between the class separator and the best separator limit, i.e. 1||w||. Maximizing 1||w|| equals to minimizing |w|2, then the search of the best separator with the biggest margin value could be formulated as the constrained optimizing problem showed by equation (4) by considering the constrain of equation (5).(4)minw=12|w|2(5)yi(xi.w+b)−1≥0

This issue would be easier to complete if it was converted into a Lagrangian formula using a Lagrange multiplier. Therefore, the issue of constraint optimization could be converted into equation (6).(6)L_(p)(w,b,α)=12||w||2−∑i=1lai(yi(xi.w+b)−1))where i = 1, 2, …, l and a≥0.

The optimum value of equation (6) could be counted by minimizing L towards w and b, therefore, ∂L(w,b,α)∂b = 0 equation (7) is obtained and from ∂L(w,b,α)∂w = 0 equation (8) is obtained.(7)∑i=1laiyi=0(8)w=∑aiyixi

The best separator field searching formula is a quadratic programming issue so that the global maximum value of ai could always be found. sec.title: Pleural effusion
sec.p: Pleural effusion is a condition where excessive fluid accumulation occurs in pleura beyond the normal limit. Such excessive fluid could be caused by two conditions: transudation and exudation. Transudation could be identified as the appearance of hydrostatic pressure change while exudation is the increase of the capillary permeability of pleura blood vessels [34]. Pleura cavity is formed by the strong serosa membrane made of mesoderm. Parietal pleura is the outermost and the one covering the inner part of the chest cavity, while the pleura visceral covers the lungs. The thickness of the pleura cavity is around 10–20 μm, containing 2–5 mL functions as a lubricant so that the lungs could inflate or breathe easily. Pleura parietal and visceral consist of a layer of mesothelial producing fluid, basalis membrane, elastic tissue, and blood vessel collagen, and lymph. Pleura membrane is semipermeable. Some fluid keeps permeating from the blood vessels to parietal pleura then it is absorbed to visceral pleura and then to lymph vessels which then return to the blood vessels. The excessive fluid would cause a disturbance if it could be absorbed by the blood vessels or the lymph. In between these layers, there is a cavity called the pleura cavum. This particular cavum is the place where the fluid is produced by the pleura layer that enables the movement when we breathe. The traffic of fluid from and into the pleura should be balanced so that the amount of pleura fluid could be maintained.

Pleura fluid in normal condition would move from capillary in parietal pleura into pleura cavity which then is absorbed back through visceral pleura. This is caused by the pressure difference between hydrostatic pressure of blood which tends to maintain the fluid to keep the fluid remain inside. In normal conditions, the difference of pleura fluid absorption through visceral pleura is bigger than the difference of fluid formation by parietal pleura and the surface of visceral pleura is bigger than parietal pleura so that, it has some ml of fluid in pleura cavity. If transudation or exudation occurs, then the fluid would be accumulated in the pleura cavity, which is called pleural effusion. By using a thoracic photo, pleural effusion could be assessed by seeing the costophrenic angles on both tips of the diaphragm. The normal angle should be sharp. If a blunt angle was found, it could be suspected that pleural effusion occurred [35]. The radiography image of the pleural effusion could be seen in Fig. 2.Fig. 2
Radiology image of pleural effusion.Fig. 2

The use of SVM in detection pleural effusion has two specific characteristics differentiating the class of pleural effusion and normal. These two special characteristics are sharpness value and slope value of pleura. The sharpness value is represented by the longest distance from the center point of pleura to the edge of the pleura image. The longest distance of the pleura image is obtained by drawing a line from the center point of the pleura image to its edge. This longest distance is called as sharpness value. Sharpness value of normal class is bigger than sharpness value of pleural effusion class. The slope value of pleura is represented by pleura's lower part gradient. The lower part gradient is obtained through linear regression on the lower part contour of the pleura image. Normal class is shown by the slope value of the pleura which is bigger than the pleural effusion class.

sec.title: Segmentation
sec.p: Segmentation is a process carried out in an image to divide the image into regions or objects. The level in object division is conducted based on the need that is required to be completed. Segmentation is the first step used before the analysis process on an image is carried out. The segmentation algorithm for the monochrome picture, in general, is based on one out of two picture characteristics containing the grayscale, i.e discontinuity, and similarity. The segmentation process examples based on discontinuity characteristics are detection of dots, lines, and edges, while the examples of similarity characteristics are thresholding, region growing, region splitting, and merging [36].

Thresholding is one of the image segmentation method separating the object and the background in an image based on the grayscale. Image region which tends to be dark would be made perfectly black with an intensity value of 0 while the image region which tends to be bright would be made perfectly white with the intensity value of 1. Therefore, the output of the segmentation process with the thresholding method is a binary image with a pixel intensity value of 0 or 1 [37]. One of the ways to extract an object from the background is by choosing this model through a threshold. The equation used to convert grayscale image into a binary image on the thresholding method is shown in equation (12).(12)g(x,y)={1,iff(x,y)≥T0,iff(x,y)<T}with f(x,y) is the function of the two variables and T is the threshold. If f(x,y) is bigger or equals to the threshold, then it would be converted into value 1 and if f(x,y) is smaller than the threshold then it would be converted into 0.

Otsu is a method of dynamic threshold selection using the maximization of the addition of the amount of foreground class variant number and background to determine the optimal threshold [38,39]. This is conducted by separating the image into two classes W1 and W2 on gray level threshold T. Therefore W1 = {0, 1, 2 …, T} and W2 = {T + 1, T + 2, … L-1} where L is the amount of total gray level from the image. If the amount of pixel on gray level of i is ni, and becomes the amount of total pixel on the given picture, then the probability of gray level of i to occur is defined in equation (13).(13)pi=niN,pi≥0,∑i=0L−1pi=1
Usually, W1 is an interesting object and W2 is the background. For the background, the probability of the two classes is shown in equation (14).(14)Pw1=∑i=0TpiandPw2=∑pi=1−Pw1
It means that W1 and W2 could be calculated as shown in equities 15 and 16.(15)μw1=∑i=0Ti*piPw1(16)μw2=∑i=T+1L−1i*piPw2
Based on equities 15 and 16, it could be derived equation (17), i.e:(17)σ2(T)=Pw1Pw2(μw1−μw2)2
The optimal threshold could be obtained by maximizing variant in class [38], i.e.:(18)T*=max0<T<L−1σ2(T)

sec.title: Method
sec.p:
The thoracic images in this study were obtained from irradiation using a conventional X-ray device, with a Toshiba Rotanode type DRX-1603B with a maximum voltage of 150 kV which was carried out in the hospital. There are 150 chest images that have dimensions of 1024 × 1024, with 75 of them labeled as pleural effusion disease and 75 labeled as normal images. For each label, we decide 50 images for training and 25 images for testing. Table 1 presents the number of thoracic images, also the number of images with pleural effusion disease (75), and the other normal images (75) that have no pleural effusion, dividing each of them into two groups: 50 (77 %) for training, and 25 (33 %) for testing.Table 1
Details of the dataset.Table 1

Pleural effusion755025
Normal755025
In this section, we will explain how to determine the region of interest (ROI), segmentation, measurement of sharpness values, measurement of slope values, and SVM training on these datasets.

sec.title: Determining ROI
sec.p:
Determining ROI aims to focus the image part that would be processed, i.e. lower left pleura image (quadrant III). This location was selected since the fluid would end up in the lower part. Actually, in the left lung, there was also fluid, but it could not be used in this method since it was blocked by the heart. ROI is determined by cutting the thorax image into quarters by taking into account the ratio of the thoracic image as shown in Fig. 3. ROI dimensions are 512 × 512 pixels.Fig. 3
The example of determining ROI. (a) Before cutting, and (b) after cutting.Fig. 3
The algorithm for getting ‘ROI’ from ‘image’ (in matlab code) is as follows:
for i = 1 : 512 for j = 1 : 512 ROI (i,j) = image (i+512,j) endend

sec.title: Segmentation
sec.p:
Furthermore, image segmentation is carried out using the thresholding method. Image segmentation aims to separate an object from its background. The output of this segmentation process is a binary image. The thresholding process is carried out by checking the gray level of each pixel in the image and determining the threshold using the Otsu method [[40], [41], [42]]. If the gray level of a pixel is less than the threshold value, the pixel color will turn black, and vice versa, if the gray level of a pixel is more than the threshold value, the pixel color will turn white. To get the threshold value using the Otsu method, we use a function that is available in the matlab library with the syntax t = graythresh (image) where t is the threshold value which is a fractional number between 0 and 1, so the threshold value for graylevel is t multiplied by 255. After segmentation, we underwent a process of filling the cavity from the lung and removing unused artefacts around the lung using morphological surgery [43,44]. Fig. 4 shows an example of segmentation results.Fig. 4
The example of the segmentation result. (a) Before segmentation, and (b) after segmentation.Fig. 4
The segmentation algorithm (in matlab code) is as follows:
t = graythresh (image1)
for i = 1 : 512
for j = 1 : 512
if immage1(i,j) ≥ t * 255;
image2(i,j) = 1;
else image2(i,j) = 0;
end;
end
end.
Where image1 is the original image and image2 is the segmented image.

sec.title: The measurement of sharpness value
sec.p:
The sharpness value of the pleura is represented by the value of the longest distance from the center of the pleura to the edge of the pleura. The search for the longest distance is done by finding the distance from the center of the pleural image to the edge of the pleural image. First, look for the center point of the pleural image and then draw a line from the center point to the edge of the pleural image at an angle of 270° to 360° (in quadrant IV) to obtain 90 distance values. Of the 90 distance values, the largest value is selected. This is what is referred to as the longest distance used as the value of the pleural sharpness. Fig. 5 shows the process of finding the value of pleural sharpness.Fig. 5
Illustration of how to measure the sharpness value.Fig. 5

sec.title: The measurement of slope value
sec.p:
Determination of the slope value of the pleura is done by finding the vertical distance between points parallel to the center point to the lower edge of the pleura. The coordinates of these meeting points are the lower contours of the pleura. At these points, a straight line is drawn using linear regression. The gradient of the line is the value of the pleural slope. Fig. 6 shows the process of finding the value of the pleural slope.Fig. 6
Illustration of how to measure the slope value.Fig. 6

sec.title: Training SVM
sec.p:
Training process was conducted using 50 thoracic images identified with pleural effusion and 50 normal images. All thoracic images had been going through determining ROI, segmentation, measurement of sharpness value, and measurement of slope value. Further, we plotted the data with axis x which is the sharpness value and axis y which is the slope value, as shown in Fig. 7.Fig. 7
Graphic of how to determine hyperplane.Fig. 7

The pattern involved in effusion class is symbolized by a diamond and the pattern in normal class is symbolized by a circle. Diamond and circle in the box are called support vector. Effusion class is divided by a line with the following line equation: f1 (x) = −0,0075 x + 1,52. Normal class is divided by a line with the following line equation: f2 (x) = −0,0067 x + 1,53. After that, the middle part shows a separator line from two classes in SVM classification with the line equation is: f3 (x) = −0,0071 x + 1525. This line is called a hyperplane. This line will later be used in testing.

sec.title: Result and discussion
sec.p:
After the hyperplane is found, in this section we test whether the hyperplane we get can classify the testing data correctly. Phase of testing was conducted using 25 thoracic images identified with pleural effusion and 25 normal. In the process of testing, these 50 thoracic images were matched with the hyperplane. If it was under the hyperplane, it means that effusion pleura was identified, but if it was above the hyperplane, it means normal. The results of testing in the form of a confusion matrix can be seen in Table 2.Table 2
Testing result.Table 2
Predicted valueActual value
EffusionNormal
Effusion25 (TP)0 (FP)
Normal2 (FN)23 (TN)

From this table we calculate the accuracy in a simple way, namely the number of predicted labels that correspond to the true label (TP + TN) divided by all data (TP + TN + FP + FN) which results is 0.96 or 96 %. Based on. We can also calculate the precision of the test results with the precision formula = TP divided by TP + FP which results is 1.0 or 100 %. Which means that all pleural effusions are classified correctly.

From the 50 images tested, we found 2 images identified with pleural effusion based on the method proposed but not matched with the label from doctor's diagnosis. The doctor's diagnosis said that both images were not identified with pleural effusion. This difference was caused by an error in determining the threshold in the segmentation process so that the image of the segmentation result encountered distortion. This distortion caused an error in determining the sharpness value and slope value. The two images are shown in Fig. 8, Fig. 9.Fig. 8
The thoracic image in case 1. (a) Before segmentation, and (b) after segmentation.Fig. 8Fig. 9
The thoracic image in case 2. (a) Before segmentation, and (b) after segmentation.Fig. 9

From Fig. 8, we could see, since the error of threshold, the tip of the pleura image was cut so that the lower part of the pleura image looked blunt. Since it was blunt, the sharpness value and slope value became small that it was identified as pleural effusion. From Fig. 9, it could be seen that since the error of threshold, the tip of the pleura figure was not cut, but narrowed so that if a line was drawn from the center, the edge of the lower tip of pleura would not be reached. As a consequence, the sharpness value and slope value became small that it was identified as pleural effusion.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In this paper, we investigate an SVM-based approach to detect pleural effusion on chest images. We formulated pleural effusion detection and implemented SVM to develop the detection algorithm. We used SVM to detect chest images whether it was identified as pleural effusion or normal. Training was performed on 100 chest images, 50 of which were identified as pleural effusion and 50 were normal. We tested the proposed method based on physician diagnosis using 50 chest images, 25 of which were identified as pleural effusion and 25 were normal. The results show that our proposed method works well with 96 % accuracy and 100 % precision. Based on the results obtained in this study, we conclude that the method we propose can be used in emergencies where doctors or medical experts are not available, while there are patients who must be treated quickly. We recommend several suggestions for further pleural effusion research, such as follow-up studies using chest images from different hospitals or different populations. The pleural effusion detection method can also be performed together with the detection of the type of pleural fluid. In addition, the SVM classification method can be used to help diagnose other diseases whose characteristics are unknown.
